extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and practitioners of political economy and banking (general readers interested in banking theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance on the proper conduct of banking, the effects of paper money and bills of exchange, and institutional precautions to preserve public and bank credit. Focuses on practical principles for banks, bankers, and governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real vs fictitious bills of exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: It was often difficult to distinguish between a real and a fictitious bill of exchange, between a bill drawn by a real creditor upon a real debtor, and a bill for which there was properly no real creditor but the bank which discounted it, nor any real debtor but the projector who made use of the money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for chains of drawing and redrawing among many correspondents that mask the absence of real underlying credit. Genuine bills arise from real commercial obligations; circulating/redrawn bills are essentially fictitious and produce a fictitious payment stream that does not replenish bank advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on repeated drawing/redrawing to raise money
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventurers sometimes raised money by drawing and redrawing bills (drawing second bills, third bills, etc.), which, repeated multiple times a year and loaded with commissions and interest, could cost the originator a high annual rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly rolling obligations (drawing bills to pay earlier ones) is expensive (examples given: costs could be 8–14% per year) and creates fragile financing. Treat rollovers as an anti-pattern: they inflate apparent liquidity but do not create real value and risk eventual collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks must detect circular discounting patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When two people continually draw and redraw upon one another and discount with the same banker, he must immediately discover what they are about and see they are trading not with capital of their own but with capital advanced to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks should monitor discounting patterns across accounts and correspondents. Relying on single-banker visibility makes detection easier; schemes that spread discounting across multiple bankers obscure detection and require interbank communication or stricter internal controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks should refuse further discounting to protect their own and public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: By refusing to discount any more, a banker might necessarily make the projectors bankrupts; but for his own interest and safety he might find it necessary to go on for some time, endeavouring to withdraw gradually, and making every day greater and greater difficulties about discounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudent banks may need to curtail lending even if it temporarily harms borrowers. Gradual withdrawal—tightening discounting terms—is advised to avoid precipitating mass bankruptcies while restoring soundness. The duty is to preserve bank and public credit over continuing imprudent credit extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: New banks must distinguish between real and circulating bills when discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: A new Scottish bank discounted scarce any distinction between real and circulating bills, advancing upon any reasonable security and issuing large quantities of notes, which produced temporary relief but aggravated long-run distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions formed to relieve distress must not indiscriminately discount all bills; failure to discriminate fuels overissue of notes and eventual insolvency. Liberal discounting without assessing real underlying value transfers fragility into the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-issuing bank notes beyond what the circulation can absorb
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper issued upon circulating bills often amounted to the whole fund destined for projects and was over and above the value of the gold and silver which would have circulated; such excess returned on the banks to be exchanged for bullion, emptying their coffers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing notes beyond the country’s capacity to absorb them leads to notes being returned for gold/silver, forcing the bank to borrow (e.g., by drawing on London). Sound practice limits issuance to what can reasonably remain in circulation without forcing continual external borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lending to known, prudent borrowers over many unknown speculative debtors
rubrics_metrics.description: A bank which lends to perhaps five hundred different people, the greater part of whom its directors can know very little about, is not likely to be more judicious in the choice of its debtors than a private person who lends among a few people he knows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks that extend credit widely without good knowledge invite loans to chimerical projectors and unprofitable undertakings. Smaller-scale private lenders may select more prudent debtors; banks should maintain underwriting standards and avoid becoming general loan-offices for speculative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit denominations of bank notes to keep paper money within dealer circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no bank notes are circulated under £10 (London) paper money confines itself to circulation between dealers. Where notes are as small as 20s. or a shilling (Scotland, North America), paper extends into dealer–consumer circulation and can banish gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate minimum note denominations to restrict paper to wholesale/dealer use; the author suggests perhaps no notes under £5 to avoid paper penetrating retail transactions and encouraging many small, unstable bankers. Low-denomination notes encourage proliferation of unsound issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper equals gold/silver only when fully convertible and payable on demand
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper money, consisting in bank notes, issued by people of undoubted credit, payable upon demand, without any condition, and, in fact, always readily paid as soon as presented, is, in every respect, equal in value to gold and silver money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure convertibility and unconditional payment on demand. Only then will prices and exchanges be as they would be under metallic currency; otherwise depreciation and divergence from bullion values occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking increases industry by making capital active, not by increasing capital
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not by augmenting the capital of the country, but by rendering a greater part of that capital active and productive than would otherwise be so, that the most judicious operations of banking can increase the industry of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate banking success by how well it converts dead stock (ready money) into productive capital (materials, tools, subsistence) rather than by nominal expansion of money supply. Prudence in operations matters more than sheer expansion of credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware systemic vulnerability when circulation is carried largely by paper
rubrics_metrics.description: An unsuccessful war in which the enemy got possession of the capital... would occasion a much greater confusion in a country where the whole circulation was carried on by paper, than in one where the greater part of it was carried on by gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High reliance on paper increases susceptibility to crises (loss of convertibility, barter, tax payment collapse). Policy should consider national security and resilience when choosing the extent of paper dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate the two branches of circulation and their money needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The circulation of every country may be considered as divided into two branches: the circulation of the dealers with one another, and the circulation between the dealers and the consumers. The former requires larger sums per transaction; the latter often small sums which circulate faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary instruments and denominations should be designed with these two circulations in mind. Large-denomination paper serves wholesale dealer transactions; small coins/notes serve retail consumer transactions. Velocity differs: small sums circulate faster and thus require less nominal stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount real bills and lend on cash-accounts rather than financing speculative projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Partly by discounting real bills of exchange, and partly by lending upon cash-accounts, banks and bankers might still be able to relieve the greater part of dealers from keeping stock in ready money; they might give the utmost assistance which banks can with propriety give to traders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor lending practices supporting genuine trade (discounting real bills, cash-account lending) rather than financing slow-return speculative improvements or grand projects whose returns are very distant. This preserves bank soundness and yields productive employment of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large banks linked to the state have special public duties and vulnerabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank of England acts not only as an ordinary bank but as a great engine of state: it receives and pays the greater part of the annuities due to public creditors, circulates exchequer bills, and advances to government taxes before collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks with state roles may be compelled by public duty to overstock circulation with paper, sometimes not through fault of directors. Their stability is tied to the state's; their operations affect national credit and may force them to take on exceptional risks for public purposes.
